title: C9 Bulbs vs Mini Lights vs Icicles: Choosing a Look for Your Home
metaTitle: C9 vs Mini Lights vs Icicles: Which Look Fits?
metaDescription: C9 bulbs, mini lights and icicle strands each create a different look on a Southern Ontario home. Here is how to choose the right style for your roofline.
excerpt: The bulb style you choose changes the entire character of a Christmas display. Here is how C9 bulbs, mini lights and icicles differ, and which suits which kind of home.
heroAlt: Comparison of a Hamilton area home lit with bold C9 bulbs along a warm brick roofline at dusk
keyTakeaways: C9 bulbs are the classic bold roofline look, large and evenly spaced, and the standard choice for commercial-grade seasonal installations across Southern Ontario.
Mini lights create a softer, denser glow, better suited to wrapping trees, shrubs and porch railings than tracing a long roofline.
Icicle lights add a hanging, dripping effect along eaves and are often paired with C9 rooflines rather than used as a stand-alone style.
The right choice depends on architecture, roofline length, and whether the display leans toward a bold classic statement or a softer, layered look.
A professional design conversation can combine all three styles in one cohesive display rather than forcing a single choice for the whole house.

body.text: Walk through any neighbourhood in Hamilton, Burlington or Oakville in December and you will notice that not every display looks the same, even on similar houses. Some homes have a bold, evenly spaced line of large bulbs tracing every roofline. Others have a softer, twinkling glow wrapped through trees and along a porch railing. Some have a curtain of lights hanging down from the eaves like icicles. These differences come down to bulb style, and choosing the right one, or the right combination, is one of the most important design decisions in any Christmas lighting project.
C9 bulbs: the classic roofline statement

C9 bulbs are the large, rounded bulbs most people picture when they imagine a classic Christmas display. Each bulb is roughly the size of a large egg, spaced at regular intervals along a strand, and when they trace a roofline they create a bold, high-contrast outline of the house that reads clearly from the street, even from a passing car. This is the standard product for most professional roofline installations, and it is what Festive Holiday Lighting installs as commercial-grade LED product on the majority of classic seasonal jobs across Southern Ontario.

C9 bulbs work particularly well on homes with strong architectural lines, such as a clear roof edge, defined gables, or a peaked porch roof, because the bold spacing highlights the shape of the house rather than competing with it. They also hold up well to a full Ontario winter. Commercial-grade LED C9 bulbs are more durable and weather-resistant than the residential strands sold seasonally at big box stores, which matters over a season that includes freeze-thaw cycles, wind, and the occasional January thaw and refreeze.
Colour options with C9

Warm white is the most popular choice for C9 rooflines, especially on brick or stone homes, because it reads as classic and elegant rather than seasonal-only, and it pairs well with almost any exterior colour. Multicolour C9 is a traditional look that leans more festive and nostalgic, and some homeowners choose a single bold colour, such as red or a cool white, to match a specific design theme. The right colour is partly personal taste and partly about what complements the home's brick, siding or stone.
Mini lights: softer, denser, better for texture

Mini lights are the small, closely spaced bulbs most commonly seen wrapped around tree trunks, woven through shrubs, or strung along a porch railing. Where C9 bulbs create a bold outline, mini lights create a denser, more textured glow, since there are far more bulbs packed into the same length of strand. This makes them the natural choice for anywhere a display calls for volume and softness rather than a sharp defined line, such as wrapping the branches of a mature tree or filling in a boxwood hedge along a front walk.

Mini lights are less commonly used to trace a long roofline on their own, since the smaller bulbs and denser spacing can look busy or washed out across a long, straight run compared with the clean line C9 bulbs provide. Where mini lights genuinely shine is in tree wraps, garland accents, and any spot in the display that benefits from a softer, twinkling texture rather than a bold outline.
Icicle lights: the hanging, dripping effect

Icicle lights are strands with multiple short drops hanging down at intervals, creating the look of icicles dripping from the eave. They add a layer of visual interest below the roofline itself, and they are especially effective on homes with a clean, straight eave line where the hanging drops have room to read clearly against the wall or window below.

Icicles are rarely the only style used on a display. More often they are paired with a C9 roofline, with the icicles hanging just below the bold outline the C9 bulbs create, giving the display two layers instead of one. On homes with dormers, bay windows, or a porch roof, icicles can also be used selectively on just those features while the main roofline stays in C9, creating variation without lighting the whole house in a single dense style.
How to think about your own home
Architecture

Homes with strong, simple roof lines, such as a straightforward two-storey with a clear eave, generally look best with a confident C9 outline, possibly paired with icicles below. Homes with more architectural detail, such as multiple gables, a wraparound porch, or several distinct rooflines, can support more variation, mixing C9 on the main lines with icicles on a feature window or porch.
Trees and landscaping

If a property has mature trees or dense shrubs near the front of the house, mini lights are almost always the right choice for those elements, layered alongside whatever roofline style is chosen. A home with three well-placed tree wraps and a clean C9 roofline often reads as more complete than a house with C9 alone, since the trees extend the display beyond just the roof edge.
The overall impression you want

Some homeowners want a bold, unmistakable classic look that reads from down the street. Others prefer something a little softer and more layered, with light spread across trees, railings and a roofline rather than concentrated in one bright outline. Neither approach is right or wrong, but naming which impression you are after early in the design conversation makes it much easier to land on the right mix of C9, mini lights and icicles for your specific property.

Most well-designed displays are not a single bulb style but a combination: C9 on the main roofline, icicles on a feature eave, and mini lights wrapped through trees and shrubs. A design conversation before installation is where these choices come together.
How the three styles compare at a glance

items: C9 bulbs: large, bold, evenly spaced. Best for tracing a clean roofline, gables and porch peaks. The standard choice for a classic, high-contrast display that reads well from the street.

Mini lights: small, dense, closely spaced. Best for wrapping tree trunks and branches, filling shrubs and hedges, and lining porch railings where a softer, textured glow suits the feature better than a bold outline.
Icicle lights: hanging drops at intervals along an eave. Best paired with a C9 roofline for a layered look, or used selectively on a single feature such as a dormer or bay window.

body.text: A note on colour temperature

Beyond the choice of bulb style, colour temperature has a real effect on how a display reads against a home's exterior. Warm white, similar to the glow of an incandescent bulb, tends to complement brick, stone and warmer siding tones, and it has become the most requested colour for both C9 rooflines and mini light tree wraps because it looks intentional and elegant rather than purely seasonal. Cool white reads brighter and crisper, and can suit homes with grey stone, dark siding or a more modern architectural style. Multicolour remains a popular traditional option, particularly for families who associate a mix of red, green, blue and gold with childhood memories of the season. None of these choices are fixed rules, and part of the value of a proper design conversation is trying out what actually looks right on your specific brick or siding tone rather than guessing from a catalogue photo.
Matching bulb style to home style

A brick two-storey with defined gables in Ancaster or Waterdown tends to suit a confident C9 outline that follows those gable lines closely, since the architecture already does most of the design work. A stone-front bungalow with a single straight eave in Grimsby often looks best with warm white C9 along that eave paired with icicles for a bit of extra depth, since there is less roofline to work with and the icicles add visual interest without overcomplicating a simple shape. A larger property in Oakville or Mississauga with several mature trees near the front of the house benefits from mini light tree wraps that extend the display beyond the roofline itself, creating a more immersive scene when viewed from the street or driveway rather than a single line of light along the top of the house.

faq.q: Which bulb style is best for a long, straight roofline?
faq.a: C9 bulbs are generally the best fit for a long, straight roofline because their bold spacing creates a clean, high-contrast line that reads clearly from the street. Mini lights tend to look busier or washed out over a long straight run compared with C9.

faq.q: Can I mix C9, mini lights and icicles on the same house?
faq.a: Yes, and most well-designed displays do exactly that. A common combination is C9 along the main roofline, icicles hanging below on a feature eave, and mini lights wrapped through trees and shrubs for added texture.

faq.q: Are icicle lights only for the roofline?
faq.a: Icicle lights are most often hung along the eave to create a dripping effect below a C9 outline, but they can also be used selectively on features like a porch roof or a dormer window rather than the entire house.

faq.q: What colour of C9 bulbs is most popular?
faq.a: Warm white is the most requested colour for C9 rooflines, particularly on brick and stone homes, since it reads as classic year after year. Multicolour and single bold colours like red are also popular for a more traditional, festive look.

faq.q: Do mini lights work well on a roofline instead of C9?
faq.a: Mini lights are better suited to trees, shrubs and railings than a long roofline, where their dense spacing can look busier than the clean, bold line C9 bulbs create. They are excellent for adding texture around a C9 roofline rather than replacing it.

faq.q: How do I decide which combination is right for my house?
faq.a: The right combination depends on your home's architecture, the trees and landscaping near the front of the house, and the overall look you want, whether bold and classic or softer and layered. A design conversation as part of a free quote at /contact is the easiest way to work through the options for your specific property.
